Individuals who are reliant on well water and those living in high-rise buildings are at a higher risk of losing water access. Potential Distributed Actions: Individuals should store one gallon of water per person for at least three days, per the CDC’s recommendation. Individuals should consider storing more if they have pets, are pregnant, or have additional health needs. Water purification tablets and filters can be used when community members have access to water but are unsure of its safety. Potential Shared Solutions: Water bottles can be distributed, or water can be collected from the tap in facilities with power. Rationale: Access to water can be severely impacted by a grid outage in a city, as most municipal water systems rely on electricity to pump and distribute water. While some water treatment plants and pumping stations have backup generators, prolonged outages can disrupt water pressure, leading to reduced or completely halted water flow. High-rise buildings are particularly vulnerable because they depend on electric pumps to deliver water to upper floors. Additionally, sewage and wastewater treatment facilities may struggle to operate without power, increasing the risk of contamination in the water supply. In some cases, authorities may issue boil water advisories if treatment systems are compromised, making access to clean drinking water even more critical. To prepare for grid outages, each household should store an emergency water supply, with at least one gallon of water per person per day for a minimum of three days. This includes water for drinking, cooking, and hygiene. Households can store water in clean, food-grade containers 44 or purchase commercially bottled water. For longer-term resilience, investing in water filtration systems, purification tablets, or a gravity-fed water filter can ensure access to safe drinking water in case of contamination. If an outage is anticipated due to severe weather, filling bathtubs and large containers with tap water beforehand can provide additional non-drinking water for flushing toilets and cleaning. Beyond storage, households should be aware of alternative water sources and conservation strategies during an outage. Collecting rainwater in barrels or large containers can supplement non-potable water needs. To minimize usage, residents should avoid unnecessary flushing, use disposable dishware to reduce washing needs, and limit bathing. Property Protection- Flooding Minimum Resilience Standard: All individuals have flood and/or renters insurance coverage and rain-readiness assessments and plans if properties are at risk of flooding or sewer backups. Vulnerability: Homes in wetland and flood plain areas are at the highest risk of flooding. Homeowners with sump pumps are vulnerable to basement flooding during times of electrical outage. Potential Distributed Actions: In the event of flooding, homeowners can prepare by sealing foundation cracks, elevating valuable items and electrical appliances in basements, and clearing gutters and downspouts to ensure water is able to be directed away from the house.
